label: In code (Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, C++ and similar) and technical prose, a list or array value being created, declared or grown: strongest for an empty list or array literal about to be filled, a list or array type or type hint, a list-producing constructor, and appending or pushing an item onto a list; prose stating that something returns or holds a list or array also fires. Merely reading an existing list (indexing one element, taking its length, passing it along) stays weak, and looping over it is moderate. The same code with a dict, map, set, tuple or NumPy array stays quiet, and the word 'list' in everyday prose with no list value behind it fires only weakly; a variable merely named like a list that holds something else (a number, string or None) sits in between, weaker than a real list but not quiet.

label_history: In code, a list or array value being made or typed (an empty or filled [] literal, list(), or a List, ArrayList or vector type, in Python, JavaScript, Java or C++), and docs saying a function returns a list; dicts, sets, tuples and plain numbers stay quiet, and so does 'list' in everyday prose.

In code (Python, JavaScript, Java, C++ and similar), a list or array being made or typed (an empty or filled [] literal, list(), or a List, ArrayList, Array or vector type or type hint) or grown by adding an item to it (append, push), plus technical text saying something returns a list. Removing items (pop), dicts, sets, tuples and plain numbers stay quiet, and so does 'list' in everyday prose; a variable that is only named with 'list' can fire weakly.

In code (Python, JavaScript, Java, C++ and similar), a list or array being started, typed or grown: strongest for an empty list literal or empty list constructor that is about to be filled, a List/ArrayList/vector type or type hint, or adding one item to the end of it (append, push); a list literal that already holds items fires more weakly, and so does technical prose saying something returns a list or array. Dicts, sets, tuples, plain numbers and 'list' in everyday prose stay quiet; a variable only named with 'list' can fire weakly.

In code or technical writing, the list data type: an empty list being created ([] or list(), ArrayList, vector, a JavaScript array), an item appended or pushed onto a list, a List type hint, a list comprehension, or prose saying a function is or returns a list (the word 'array' in prose fires more weakly). The word 'list' in everyday or non-programming senses (a ship listing, a stock listing, shopping or guest lists) stays quiet, as do dicts, sets and tuples in the same code. A variable whose name contains 'list' fires moderately even when it does not hold a list.

In code (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, C++ and similar) and technical prose, a value that is a list or array, whether it is being built or only used: strongest for an empty list or array literal about to be filled and for a list/array type or type hint, but it also fires on adding an item to a list, on expressions or calls that produce a list, on reading, passing or looping over a variable that holds a list (often a plural name), and on prose saying something returns or holds a list or array. The same code with a dict, set, tuple, string or single number or object stays quiet. The word 'list' alone (in everyday prose, or in a variable name whose value is not a list) fires weakly to moderately.

In code (Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Java, C++ and similar) and technical prose, a list or array value being created, declared or grown: strongest for an empty list or array literal about to be filled, a list or array type or type hint, a list-producing constructor, and appending or pushing an item onto a list; prose stating that something returns or holds a list or array also fires. Merely reading an existing list (indexing one element, taking its length, passing it along) stays weak, and looping over it is moderate. The same code with a dict, map, set, tuple or NumPy array stays quiet, and the word 'list' with no list value behind it (everyday prose, or a variable named like a list that holds something else) fires only weakly.
